sub_question: SQ3: How do specific pollutants affect respiratory illness (asthma, COPD)?
summary: A 59-study meta-analysis confirms short-term exposure to all major pollutants significantly raises COPD exacerbation risk, with NO2 (RR 1.04, 95% CI 1.03-1.06) and O3 (RR 1.03, 1.01-1.04) per 10 µg/m³ the strongest gaseous drivers; PM raises risk too. Shared mechanism = oxidative stress + airway inflammation. Critically, gaseous pollutants peak at lag0 (same day) and particulates at lag3 (3-day delay).
key_insight: Two agent-actionable facts: (1) NO2 and O3 are the dominant COPD-exacerbation triggers among gases — the agent should weight them heavily for COPD users (NO2=traffic proxy, O3=hot sunny afternoons). (2) The LAG STRUCTURE is a design gift: gaseous effects hit same-day (lag0) so alerts must be real-time, but PARTICULATE effects peak ~3 days later (lag3) — meaning the agent can WARN a PM-sensitive patient days ahead of their symptom peak, and should attribute today's symptoms to particulate exposure from ~3 days prior.

detail.asthma_note: PM2.5 linked to asthma development AND exacerbation via oxidative stress (per parallel sources: PMC9001082, PMC10990824); ozone worsens asthma airway reactivity (EPA).

notes: COPD RR values from the 59-study Li et al. 2016 meta-analysis (Int J COPD). Mechanism corroborated across meta-analysis + PM2.5-asthma oxidative-stress review + EPA ozone/asthma page. Asthma-specific quantitative RRs not yet pulled per-pollutant — could deepen later but mechanism + development link is established.
